templateNote: One frame per pipeline stage (retrieval signals, fusion and candidates, reranking, generation) plus one for the measured trade-offs; labelled flows_to links carry what passes between stages. The summary may be a card outside the frames or a frame takeaway.

frames.title: Retrieval signals: keywords and embeddings
frames.purpose: The two retrievers side by side, each with its strength and its weakness.
frames.rationale: BM25 and embeddings are two answers to one question (how to find candidate passages); their weaknesses are each other's strengths, which a side-by-side frame shows.

frames.title: Fusion and candidates
frames.purpose: How the two lists become one candidate list: the hybrid idea with its condition, the RRF formula, and the candidate budget.
frames.rationale: Hybrid search, RRF and candidate generation are one step of the pipeline (merge for recall).

separateFrom.reason: Fusion merges for recall; reranking reorders for precision. Mixing them blurs the trade-off.

frames.title: Reranking
frames.purpose: What the cross-encoder does, and what reranking does and doesn't buy.
frames.rationale: The step and its critical limitation belong together; the limitation is about this step only.

separateFrom.reason: The reranker is not a third retriever: it can only reorder what retrieval found.

frames.title: Generation
frames.purpose: Why retrieval bounds the answer, how the model uses the top passages, and the worked example.
frames.rationale: The main claim (the answer can be no better than retrieval) is about generation's input; the example ends in a generated answer.

frames.title: Relevance, latency and cost
frames.purpose: The measured table and the latency price of reranking, with the caveat on the figures.
frames.rationale: The numbers compare configurations across stages, so they sit in their own frame rather than inside any one stage.

elements.content: BM25 finds exact terms and rare identifiers (E-4012, sync.retry_window) — but misses passages that use different words
Embeddings find passages that mean the same thing — but are weak on exact codes (missed 31 of 50 error-code queries)
Hybrid search can improve recall — when the lexical and semantic signals are complementary; otherwise it adds latency for little gain
elements.layout: The condition is part of this card, never a card of its own.

elements.content: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: each passage scores 1/(k + rank) per list, summed; k = 60
Top 50 from each retriever, at most 100 fused candidates; tuned for recall, not precision
A cross-encoder reads query and passage together, rescoring only the fused candidates; the top 8 are kept
Reranking improves the precision of the top results — it does not guarantee a correct answer and can only reorder what retrieval found
elements.layout: The limitation is part of this card, never a card of its own.

elements.content: RAG retrieves, then generates; the model never sees the rest of the collection, so the answer is bounded by retrieval
The model answers only from the top 8 passages, cites them, and says so when none applies
Example: 'What does E-4012 mean?' — BM25 finds the error-code table, vectors the resumable-uploads article; both reach the top 8
Configuration × correct passage in top 8 × median latency × cost per 1,000 queries (61/68/79/88%, 35–190 ms, $0.02–$0.95)
Reranking adds about 120 ms per query and most of the cost — figures from one collection and one query set
Hybrid widens the net, reranking sorts the catch, generation can only work with what it is given; each helps only under its own conditions
elements.outsideFrameReason: The takeaway spans every stage, so it belongs to no single frame: a summary card beside the frames (or a frame takeaway).

relationships.explanation: BM25 contributes its top 50 passages to the candidate list.
Vector retrieval contributes its top 50 passages to the candidate list.
The candidate list is the RRF-fused list.
The fused candidates are what the cross-encoder rescores.
The reranker hands the top 8 passages to the language model.
The worked example ends in a generated answer from the top 8.

together.reason: The two retrieval signals are compared side by side.
Hybrid search, its fusion formula and the candidate budget are one merge step.
The reranking step and what it does and doesn't buy.
The example ends in a generated answer.

keepSeparate.reason: Reranking reorders what retrieval found; putting it among the retrievers suggests it can find passages itself.
Both are encoder models, but one retrieves from the whole collection and the other only rescores candidates.

hierarchy.reason: The example illustrates the pipeline's output and must not read as a main idea.

unsupported.ideal: Each card cites its units: bm25 u4–u9; vector u10–u15; hybrid u16–u18; rrf u19–u22; candidates u23–u25; cross-encoder u26–u30; rerank u31–u33; generation u34–u36; example u37; table u38–u40; latency u41–u43; rag-bound u1–u2; summary u44–u45.
unsupported.expectedToday: Not checkable; cards carry no citations. Matching is by content.

unsupported.ideal: A deterministic rule flags a hedge turned into an absolute ('can improve' → 'always improves') or a dropped 'does not guarantee'.
unsupported.expectedToday: Approximated by text_absent / text_present assertions on the plan.

unsupported.ideal: The example is styled as an example, the caveats as caveats.
unsupported.expectedToday: Plain cards; lower importance on the example is the only signal.
